title: Finding The Hippo Attack Annoying? TRY THIS!! | GM Naroditsky’s Top Theory Speedrun

moves.spoken: The opponent trolls with a quiet e3 and d3 — a Hippo-style setup where White fianchettoes both bishops and tucks the knights back toward e2 and d2. It's worth knowing a sustainable way to punish these off-beat systems, because a lot of players either get scared or start stumbling against them.
Since White is handing us the centre, we grab it — the principled e5.
And we grab more with d5, taking a big share of the middle.

The preferred setup refrains from the knight to c6. Instead c6 builds a solid pawn chain, and the queen's knight reroutes Ruy-Lopez style via d7 and f8 to g6. Against such unambitious play, we have all the time in the world to improve.
teaches: the c6 chain and knight reroute

moves.spoken: The bishop to d6 complements c6 beautifully — London-style. It defends the e5-pawn while the pawn defends d5, giving us a super-compact, well-placed centre.
Castle kingside — never queenside here, that's far too adventurous. And note White's h3 is already a slight weakness; if g3 follows, it only creates another target on that wing.
teaches: castle kingside, note the h3 weakness

moves.spoken: Temper your expectations against these setups. I've seen countless games where one side plays an offbeat system and the other charges straight for the throat and loses — White isn't doing anything to lose the game. Be patient, get every piece out, and accept that breaking such a setup down takes time; it can't be done in the opening.
A typical queenside idea is to advance the a-pawn to poke and prod — and if White answers b4, we chip in with c5. With a closed centre, don't rule out moving the same pawn twice; there's no hurry.

Leave the light-squared bishop at home for now — a bishop to f5 walks into a g4 or e3-e4 expansion, and a bishop to e6 invites a knight jump to g5. We want to keep that bishop, because a key middlegame plan is pressuring the h3-pawn. So develop the knight to d7 instead.
teaches: keep the light bishop for the h3 plan

moves.spoken: The rook to e8 overprotects the e5-pawn — a good move in its own right — while we continue rerouting the knight toward g6.

If White's queen slides to e2, it signals a flirtation with castling queenside — a near-suicidal plan into our setup. So we play a5, telling the opponent: don't you dare castle into this, because we'll be ready to make mincemeat of that king.
